displayQuote: If you can dream it, you can do it

meta.title: Who really said "If you can dream it, you can do it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Walt Disney never said it. Disney's own archivist found no record. The line was written for Epcot's Horizons in 1983 — and even that authorship is contested.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you can dream it, you can do it'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Walt Disney. Disney's archivist found no record of it. Imagineer Tom Fitzgerald wrote it for Epcot's Horizons (1983) — though a GE copywriter disputes even that.

answer.label: Not Walt Disney — claimed by
answer.authorDates: Walt Disney Imagineer · wrote the Horizons script, Epcot, 1983
answer.sourceLine: Walt Disney never said this. Disney’s own archivist, Dave Smith, checked and found no record of it — the line was written for Horizons, the General Electric–sponsored Epcot pavilion that opened in 1983, seventeen years after Walt’s death. Imagineer Tom Fitzgerald told Smith flatly: “I am very familiar with that line because I wrote it!” At the ride it read “If we can dream it, we can do it.” A copywriter named Sheralyn Silverstein separately claims she coined the “you” wording in 1981 for a GE recruitment campaign — credible and endorsed by historian Jim Korkis, and GE brochures and recruitment ads printed in 1982, a year before Horizons opened, carry the exact “you” wording; no artifact dated to the 1981 writing itself has surfaced.
answer.confidenceText: Ruled out for Walt Disney by the Disney Archives; the true originator is contested between a Disney Imagineer and a GE ad copywriter.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: “If we can dream it, we can do it” — not the “you” form

source.excerpt: Despite its frequent publication, that is not a Walt Disney quote. We checked with Imagineer Tom Fitzgerald for the definitive answer: “I am very familiar with that line because I wrote it! It was written specifically for the Horizons attraction at Epcot and used in numerous ways, from dialogue in the ride to graphics. I find it amusing that the Science of Imagineering DVD series attributes it to Walt Disney, but I guess I should be flattered.”
trail: 1981 — the disputed first draft. Copywriter Sheralyn Silverstein says she wrote “If you can dream it, you can do it” in 1981 at the Marsteller agency for a General Electric recruitment campaign, framed as a teacher's line to a student. Surviving GE brochures and recruitment ads printed in 1982 — reproduced in the interview — carry the exact “you” wording ↗, a year before Horizons opened. Her agency president, Lou Magnani, told her that Jack Welch walked to the wall, pointed at her line and said “That's the reason I'm going to sign your agency!” — Silverstein was too junior to be in the room, so that scene reaches us second-hand. No artifact dated to the 1981 writing itself has surfaced, so the precise date of composition rests on her account.

1983 — the line goes up at Epcot. The GE-sponsored Horizons pavilion opens on 1 October with “If we can dream it, we can do it” as its thesis. Attractions Magazine places it in the entry hallway, the ride dialogue, and the post-1995 score ↗ — and notes GE sponsored the pavilion, the same client Silverstein was writing for.

2008 — Disney credits Walt. Disney's own Science of Imagineering DVD series (Disney Educational Productions, launched 2008) attributes the line to Walt Disney — the credit Fitzgerald singled out when he told the Archives he found it “amusing… but I guess I should be flattered.” Gizmodo lists it among Walt Disney quotes that are simply fake ↗.

2013 — the archives rule. Dave Smith publishes Fitzgerald's denial in Ask Dave; Wikiquote's Misattributed section adopts it as the definitive answer ↗. The line nonetheless remains on Disney-licensed merchandise under Walt's name.
source.excerptNote: Dave Smith — Disney's founding archivist — answering the question directly in his Ask Dave column (D23, 2013), quoting Fitzgerald. The original D23 page is now offline; the text survives via Wikiquote ↗, which also cites Smith's Disney Trivia from the Vault (2012), p. 243.
source.rightsNote: This is not a public-domain line. Every documented version of it is a 1980s corporate work — either a 1981 General Electric recruitment campaign written at the Marsteller agency or the 1983 Horizons script for Walt Disney Imagineering — and the two claimants disagree about which came first, so we cannot identify the originating work with confidence. Note separately that short taglines of this kind generally fall below the threshold of copyright protection in the United States regardless of authorship; the live question here is credit, not licensing.

author.name: Tom Fitzgerald
author.kicker: Not the founder — the staff writer
author.heading: The Imagineer who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: Walt Disney Imagineer · 40+ years at WED/Imagineering · writer of Epcot's Horizons (1983)
author.bio: Tom Fitzgerald spent more than four decades at Walt Disney Imagineering, becoming one of the most influential creative leaders in the company's history. In the early 1980s he wrote the script for Horizons, the General Electric–sponsored Epcot pavilion, whose thesis line — “If we can dream it, we can do it” — ran through the entry hallway, the ride dialogue, and the score. When the line began circulating as Walt Disney's, Fitzgerald's reaction was wry rather than proprietary: “I guess I should be flattered.”

Not Walt Disney — the Disney Archives found no record of him saying it.

misattribution.heading: How a ride tagline became a founder's motto
misattribution.intro: This is the rare fake quote that Disney's own archives debunked — and that Disney itself keeps selling. It is arguably the single most-repeated line falsely credited to Walt Disney.

items.why: Disney's founding archivist, Dave Smith, addressed the question directly in his Ask Dave column: “Despite its frequent publication, that is not a Walt Disney quote.” Wikiquote files it under Misattributed ↗ on that authority. Walt Disney died in 1966; the line is documented only from the 1980s.

The version at Epcot was collective: “If we can dream it, we can do it.” Attractions Magazine documents that form ↗ in the pavilion's entry hallway, ride dialogue, and post-1995 score. The familiar “you” wording is not the Horizons line.

The misattribution was propagated by Disney itself — Fitzgerald noted it was the Science of Imagineering DVD series that credited the line to Walt, adding “I guess I should be flattered.” AllEars reports Disney still markets it on merchandise as Walt's ↗ despite zero evidence.

Fitzgerald told the Disney Archives he wrote it for Horizons. But copywriter Sheralyn Silverstein says she coined the “you” wording in 1981 at Marsteller for a General Electric recruitment campaign — and GE sponsored Horizons. Of Fitzgerald's claim she says: “I respectfully say he is incorrect” ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The one thing every source agrees on: it isn't Walt's. Disney historian Jim Korkis leads his catalogue of fake Walt quotes with this one ↗ — and on the deeper question of who wrote it, Korkis concludes: “it seems like Silverstein should get credit for the line that we all know today” ↗.

context.heading: A corporate tagline that grew into a founder's creed
lead: Horizons was Epcot's thesis statement in ride form — a General Electric–sponsored optimism machine about the future that families rode from 1983 into the late 1990s. Its message was communal by design: “If we can dream it, we can do it.” The pronoun mattered. It was a promise about what people could build together, sponsored by the company that wanted to hire them.

The line drifted. Somewhere between the pavilion wall and the internet, “we” became “you,” a collective promise became a personal one, and an anonymous staff writer's tagline was reassigned to the most quotable man in the building. By 2008 Disney's own Science of Imagineering DVD series was printing it as Walt's — and Disney has since sold it on merchandise under his name.
context.detailsSummary: Why this one sticks so well
detailsBody: The misattribution survives because it is plausible. The sentiment genuinely echoes Walt Disney's public philosophy, and the line was born inside a Disney park — so it carries real Disney DNA even though Walt had nothing to do with it. That is the hardest kind of fake quote to dislodge: not a fabrication from nowhere, but a house-style line that got promoted to the founder.

Similar sentiments long predate both men. Gizmodo notes the resemblance to Napoleon Hill's Depression-era formula about what the mind can conceive and believe, it can achieve — a reminder that “who first said it” and “who first phrased it this way” are different questions.
context.pull: Walt Disney died in 1966. Horizons opened in 1983.
